passage: At home in the flat, Naveen, five, held up a spoon of peas. "If I eat peas, can I have a sticker?" His father Suraj smiled. "Peas first. Stickers are for the chart on Sundays." "Just one sticker. Please. One." "Not tonight. But if you eat a few peas, you can pick the bedtime story." Naveen counted five peas into his mouth. "Story!"

qa.q: What did Naveen want in return for eating peas?
What might Naveen be feeling as he offers the trade, and what does he want?
qa.a: He is probably hopeful and eager to get a sticker for eating peas he dislikes. He may also have been testing whether the trade would work.

qa.q: How did Suraj hold the limit kindly?
qa.a: He said no to the sticker but offered a different reward, picking the bedtime story.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel about the trade?
qa.a: Probably amused and patient, since he smiled and offered another option.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pleading and offering a simple bargain, with a parent holding the limit kindly and rewarding flexibility.

passage:
"Please, one more turn!" said Nitin, five, on the park slide.
"The timer's done. Time to go," said his mother Hafsa.
"I'll give you my biscuit if I get one more turn."
Hafsa laughed. "A biscuit for a turn? That's a clever trade, but it's time to go home."
"Then tomorrow I go first?"
"Tomorrow you can have the first turn, if we come at our usual time."
"Deal!"

qa.q: What does Nitin's offer of the biscuit suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: That he is trying a trade to get what he wants, showing a growing sense of exchange. He might also have been worried about the fun ending.

qa.q: How did Hafsa keep the limit and still reward flexibility?
qa.a: She said it was time to go now but agreed to a first turn tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about Nitin's trade?
qa.a: Amused, since she laughed, though she stayed firm.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pleading and bargaining for one more turn, with a parent holding the limit and offering a fair alternative.
